## Why model individuals?

- An ABM stores each individual's status, so the population counts are
  something we compute rather than the model's only state.
- Contact rules can be changed without deriving a new aggregate equation.
- Who contacts whom *can* be made explicit, but only if you record it.

This unit uses a stochastic, discrete-time, discrete-state, individual-level
model with $\Delta t=0.1$, $c=10$, $\beta=0.05$, and $\gamma=0.25$.

::: {.notes}
The model is well mixed rather than spatial.  That keeps the connection to the
SIR equations visible before adding networks or households.

Be careful with the third bullet: this implementation does *not* log contacts or
transmission sources.  They exist during an update and are discarded.  Recording
who infected whom needs an event history or extra agent fields.  Worth saying
aloud, because "ABMs track who infected whom" is a common overstatement.
:::

## Individual transition probabilities

For $K_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ contacts,
$$
\Pr(S\to I\mid I_t)=1-\exp\left[-c\Delta t\,\beta I_t/N\right].
$$
Recovery uses
$$
\Pr(I\to R)=1-\exp(-\gamma\Delta t).
$$
In the large-population limit, with $\Delta t$ small, the aggregate behaviour is
$$
\dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\quad
\dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\quad
\dot R=\gamma I.
$$

::: {.notes}
The Poisson contact calculation explains why the ABM's well-mixed rule
approximates mass action while retaining individual randomness.

Both limits are needed, and it is worth naming them separately.  Letting
$\Delta t\to0$ on its own removes the frozen-step error and leaves the
continuous-time stochastic process for this same finite population, whose
ensemble mean is not the ODE.  The ODE arrives only when $N$ is large as well.

The last part of the worksheet depends on exactly the finite-population
behaviour that the large-$N$ limit throws away, so promising the ODE here would
set up an agreement the room will not find.
:::

## Agents.jl 7 model logic

```{julia}
#| echo: true
using Agents, CairoMakie, Distributions, StableRNGs

@agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

function model_step!(model)
    for p in allagents(model)
        p.status = p.next_status
    end
end

susceptible_count(model) = count(p.status == :S for p in allagents(model))
infected_count(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))
recovered_count(model) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(model))

function agent_step!(p, model)
    p.next_status = p.status
    if p.status == :S
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c*model.Δt))
            q = random_agent(model)
            if q.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                p.next_status = :I; break
            end
        end
    elseif p.status == :I &&
           rand(abmrng(model)) < 1-exp(-model.γ*model.Δt)
        p.next_status = :R
    end
end
```

The second field makes the update synchronous.

::: {.notes}
Without `next_status`, activation order could let an agent infected early in a
step transmit during that same step.  That would be an unintended scheduling
assumption.
:::

## Current-code result

```{julia}
#| echo: true
model = StandardABM(Person; agent_step!, model_step!,
    properties=(β=0.05, c=10.0, γ=0.25, Δt=0.1),
    rng=StableRNG(20250711))
for id in 1:200
    status = id <= 5 ? :I : :S
    add_agent!(Person(; id, status, next_status=status), model)
end
_, data = run!(model, 200; mdata=[susceptible_count,
    infected_count, recovered_count], showprogress=false)
counts = Matrix(data[:, [:susceptible_count, :infected_count,
    :recovered_count]])'
(peak_I=maximum(counts[2,:]),
    population_error=maximum(abs.(sum(counts; dims=1) .- 200)))
```

The result is generated from the current `run!` API.  Conservation should be
exact even though the infectious curve is random.

::: {.notes}
The small population keeps a slide render quick.  The Pluto notebook exposes
population, initial infections, contact rate, and horizon as controls.
:::

## Space, and what a neighbourhood is

A space decides which agents are near which others. Grids, graphs, continuous
space, street maps, or your own. What the rules consult is the
**neighbourhood**, fixed by two choices:

- the **radius**, how far a person looks;
- the **metric**, how distance is counted. On a grid `:chebyshev` counts a
  diagonal as one step, so radius 1 is the eight surrounding cells.

A periodic grid wraps, so everyone has the same number of neighbours; a bounded
one gives people near an edge fewer.

::: {.notes}
This is the slide the worksheet is built on, so spend time here rather than on
the API.  The point to land is that "neighbourhood" is not a vague word: it is
exactly two numbers, and both are modelling choices that change the answer.

The bounded-versus-periodic point is worth a sentence aloud.  With edges, a
corner agent has three neighbours instead of eight, so the epidemic is damped
near the boundary for a reason that has nothing to do with the disease.
:::

## The neighbourhood, drawn {.smaller}

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| label: fig-slide-ch06-neighbourhood
#| fig-cap: "Chebyshev radius 1 (dark red), radius 2 adds the orange cells."
@agent struct GridPerson(GridAgent{2})
    status::Symbol
end

grid = StandardABM(GridPerson,
    GridSpaceSingle((9, 9);
        periodic=false,
        metric=:chebyshev);
    model_step! = (m -> nothing),
    rng=StableRNG(1))

for p in positions(grid)
    add_agent!(p, grid; status=:S)
end

focal = grid[id_in_position((5, 5), grid)]
r1 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, grid, 1))
r2 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, grid, 2))

colour(p) = p.id == focal.id ? :black :
            p.id in r1 ? :firebrick :
            p.id in r2 ? :orange : :lightgrey

fig, ax, _ = abmplot(grid; agent_color=colour,
    agent_marker=:rect, agent_size=11,
    figure=(; size=(300, 300)))
hidedecorations!(ax)
fig
```

::: {.notes}
Eight at radius 1, twenty-four at radius 2.  Ask the room which of the two they
would call "the people you meet" before saying that the worksheet uses radius 2,
and that the choice between them decides whether a single introduction can
establish at all.
:::

## Extensions and checks

- With contacts drawn from a fixed neighbourhood, $\beta c/\gamma$ is the
  mass-action reproduction number and no longer the model's $R_0$.
- Run seeded replicates, but say *which* summary you compare with the ODE.
- Measure timestep error with a deterministic map, not a small ensemble.

ABMs can represent clustering, households, behavior, and networks, but those
mechanisms introduce parameters that may be difficult to observe or identify.

::: {.notes}
An ABM is not automatically more realistic.  The contact mechanism and
calibration target determine whether its extra detail is useful.

On the second bullet: in the well-mixed model the peak of the ensemble mean and
the mean of the per-replicate peaks straddle the ODE peak, 144.9 and 168.6
against 158.5, and neither converges to it at finite $N$: averaging and
maximizing do not commute.  That straddling does not carry over to the grid model
the worksheet builds.  With contacts drawn locally every summary falls well below
the ODE peak: single runs there peak between 76 and 87 against the same 158.5.

On the third: a 16-path ensemble has a standard error of several people, so it
cannot resolve a timestep error of that size, and failing to resolve one is not
evidence of its absence.
:::

## Takeaways and links

- Agent state makes contact and scheduling assumptions explicit.
- Synchronous updates protect the intended discrete-time semantics.
- Aggregate validation must be paired with checks of the individual rule.
